clue.text: In which state Proust wouldn't remember anything past?

definitions.text: In which state Proust wouldn't remember anything past?

indicators.note: the novelist's name is put into a different state, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A literary teaser: in what condition would the author of Remembrance of Things Past forget everything?
explanation.walkthrough: 'In which state' rearranges PROUST. The whole clue is also the definition: someone in a daze recalls nothing, a joke on Proust's novel À la recherche du temps perdu, known in English as Remembrance of Things Past.
explanation.definitionFit: A daze of near-unconsciousness leaves a person unable to recall anything, the opposite of Proust's famous memory.

clue.text: See to introducing play about robots

indicators.note: the word 'to' takes the play into its middle, so it holds the other piece

parts.note: taken as written
R.U.R. is Karel Čapek's 1920 play that gave us the word 'robot'

explanation.surface: An instruction to arrange for a robot play to be staged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is a noun, a bishop's diocese: Truro is the cathedral city of Cornwall and seat of a bishop.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral city in Cornwall, it is the seat of an Anglican diocese, which is what a bishop's see is.

clue.text: After birthday, total span is reduced

indicators.note: reduced in the sense of broken down into pieces, so the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gloomy remark that once you have had a birthday your total lifespan is shorter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is reduced' is the anagram signal, as in reduced to fragments, not made smaller. 'After birthday' is a loose definition: the period after the day of birth.
explanation.definitionFit: The medical adjective describes the weeks following delivery of a baby, the time after the day of birth.

clue.text: Complained at statement of old artillery commandant?

explanation.surface: Someone grumbled at what a former Royal Artillery commander announced.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is cryptic: an old commander of the Royal Artillery (RA) could say 'RA, I led'. 'Railed at' means scolded.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail at someone is to protest bitterly, and a former head of the Royal Artillery would state 'RA, I led'.

clue.text: Legitimate article in the Church of France

indicators.note: the article goes inside the French phrase for the church

parts.note: French for 'the church' is l'église
'a' is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Something declared lawful within the French Catholic Church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Legitimate' is a verb here: to make lawful.
explanation.definitionFit: To legitimate something is to make it lawful, a synonym of the verb meaning to authorise by statute.

clue.text: Discharge for sudden refusal to work

explanation.surface: Electricity let loose, or a walkout called without warning.
explanation.definitionFit: A bolt from a thunderstorm is an electrical discharge, and a walkout called at no notice is a sudden industrial stoppage.

clue.text: Previous state of gangster's moll?

parts.note: a moll is a gangster's girl, and a gangster is a hood, so the hood's girl is jokingly her earlier condition of youth

explanation.surface: Asking what a mobster's girlfriend was before she fell in with crime.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'gangster's moll' as 'hood's girl', turned round; the earlier stage of any woman's life is her time as a young girl.
explanation.definitionFit: The years before womanhood are a female's youth, the previous state of any adult woman.

clue.text: Roman poet referring to the Gospel

explanation.surface: A Latin poet whose work alludes to the New Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucan wrote the epic Pharsalia, and the adjective means relating to St Luke or his Gospel.

clue.text: Slough produced this traitor, on the surface

parts.note: a snake in the grass is a treacherous person
skin is the outer surface of a body

explanation.surface: The Berkshire town of Slough apparently produced a turncoat who seems respectable on the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough looks like the English town; here it is the cast-off outer layer a serpent sheds.
explanation.definitionFit: A serpent's slough is the old outer layer it sheds, so a slough is made of that reptile's hide.

clue.text: Outlaw to hang on to his weapons

parts.note: guns are a cowboy's weapons
to linger is to hang on or stay put

explanation.surface: A bandit determined to keep hold of his firearms.
explanation.definitionFit: A Wild West gunfighter was typically a lawless bandit.

clue.text: Many were buried in the soil

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a crossword way to say many
the dead lay buried, the past tense of lie

explanation.surface: Lots of people were interred in the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy sticky earth is a kind of ground, a type of soil.

clue.text: Gloomy start to the music

explanation.surface: A sombre opening to a piece of music.
explanation.definitionFit: Pessimistic means gloomy, and in music it is the first, accented beat of a bar.

clue.text: Watch Orion, for example

explanation.surface: Telling someone to look at the constellation of Orion.
explanation.definitionFit: A pocket timepiece with a hinged cover is so called, and Orion is the great huntsman of Greek myth and the sky.

clue.text: Clothes fit

explanation.surface: Garments that fit well.
explanation.definitionFit: A matching jacket and trousers is a set of clothes, and to be appropriate for is to fit.

clue.text: One heretic, or another

parts.note: a unit is a single thing, one
an Arian followed Arius, who denied Christ's full divinity

explanation.surface: Someone who is a heretic, or perhaps a different kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' means another heretic: Unitarians reject the Trinity, which orthodox churches judge heretical.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of a church rejecting the Trinity are, to orthodox Christians, a further variety of heretic.

clue.text: Wellington's firm hand

parts.note: iron means unyielding, firm
dukes is slang for fists or hands

explanation.surface: The Duke of Wellington's steady hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The Duke of Wellington was nicknamed the Iron Duke; 'dukes' (fists) is old boxing slang, from rhyming slang 'Duke of Yorks' for forks, meaning fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: The first Duke of Wellington, victor of Waterloo, was famously nicknamed for his resolve.

clue.text: Exhausted at last one's flow of conversation

indicators.note: only the final letter of the word before it is wanted

parts.note: one is I, and the 's is S
a course is the flow or run of a stream

explanation.surface: Worn out, someone finally pours out a stream of talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoken exchange or extended talk on a subject is a synonym of conversation.

clue.text: Colin has rewritten letters for Father Christmas

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are written out again in a new order

explanation.surface: A boy rewrites his letter to Santa.
explanation.walkthrough: Father Christmas is St Nicholas, origin of Santa Claus.
explanation.definitionFit: Santa Claus derives from the fourth-century bishop St Nicholas, patron of children.

clue.text: Submissive bearing

explanation.surface: A meek manner or demeanour.
explanation.definitionFit: A compliant person gives way readily, and a tree producing fruit is said to be cropping or bearing.

clue.text: Lied to child, glibly at first

parts.note: a son is a child

indicators.note: just the opening letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: Someone told fibs to a child, speaking glibly at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lied' is not the past of lie: it is the German word for an art song, as in Schubert's Lieder.
explanation.definitionFit: A German Lied is a solo art song, especially of the Romantic era.

clue.text: Courage — Dutch?

explanation.surface: Is this bravery merely Dutch courage?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' is British slang for nerve; 'Dutch courage' is bravery found in drink, which comes from the bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang nerve is called this, and Dutch courage, bravado from alcohol, comes from a flask of spirits.

clue.text: Start to put a lock round leper

indicators.note: only the first letter of the following word is used
the word for a lock is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: a lock is a tress of hair

explanation.surface: Instructions to fasten a padlock around a person with leprosy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leper' is figurative here: anyone shunned, not literally someone with the disease. 'round' is the reversal signal on the lock word.
explanation.definitionFit: A leper is used figuratively for an outcast shunned by society, the same as an untouchable.

clue.text: Celts get Hindu sage back to front

indicators.note: the back letter of the sage's title is moved to the front

parts.note: a rishi is a Hindu holy sage or seer

explanation.surface: Celtic people acquire an Indian guru who is wearing his clothes reversed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back to front' moves the last I of RISHI to the start.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of Ireland are among the Celtic nations, so they are Celts.

clue.text: All-embracing, albeit incomplete

parts.note: tho is an informal short spelling of though, meaning albeit
a rough draft is unfinished, incomplete

explanation.surface: Comprehensive, although not finished.
explanation.definitionFit: Comprehensive and complete in every detail means the same as all-embracing.

clue.text: Windy chap is out of the way

indicators.note: the chap is outside the way, wrapping round it

parts.note: a guy is a chap
St is an abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A man is told to stop obstructing the path.
explanation.definitionFit: Blustery weather with sudden blasts of wind is windy.

clue.text: Parrot almost gets part in opera

indicators.note: the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: to parrot is to mimic

explanation.surface: A parrot is nearly given a role in an opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Mimi is the heroine of Puccini's La Bohème.
explanation.definitionFit: The consumptive seamstress in Puccini's La Bohème is a leading role in an opera.

clue.text: Set trial, do badly, get buried

indicators.note: something done badly is muddled, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A court hearing is scheduled, goes poorly, and someone ends up in the grave.
explanation.definitionFit: A euphemism for interred, the phrase is used of the dead at a funeral.

clue.text: Not wooed, we hear, because immoral?

indicators.note: the word for not wooed is pronounced, giving a word spelt differently

parts.note: a woman not chased by suitors is unchased

explanation.surface: Was she unpursued by men because she was considered loose?
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking chastity, sexually loose, is a sense of immoral.

clue.text: Diarist regularly puts name at the end

indicators.note: the name letter is put somewhere else in the word for regularly
the new place for the moved letter is the final position

parts.note: evenly means at regular intervals

explanation.surface: A diary writer routinely signs his name at the end of each entry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puts' and 'at the end' move the N of EVENLY to the back. John Evelyn was a 17th-century English diarist.
explanation.definitionFit: John Evelyn kept a celebrated journal of seventeenth-century English life.
